passages.t: The LORD rides into Egypt, and the Nile dries up
passages.happening:
‘This is the burden against Egypt: Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud; He is coming to Egypt’ (verse 1). The idols of Egypt tremble and the Egyptians' hearts melt.

God will set Egyptian against Egyptian, brother against brother, city against city, kingdom against kingdom (verse 2). Their spirit will drain away; they will turn to idols, the spirits of the dead, mediums and spiritists (verse 3). ‘I will deliver the Egyptians into the hands of harsh masters, and a fierce king will rule over them’ (verse 4).

‘The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty’ (verse 5). The canals will stink, the reeds wither, and the fields along the Nile blow away (verses 6-7). The fishermen mourn (verse 8). The workers in flax and the weavers of fine linen are dismayed, and the hired workers are sick at heart (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 18 ended with distant Cush bringing gifts to Zion. Chapter 19 turns to Egypt, which the Cushite kings now ruled, and which Judah's leaders kept trusting as a shield against Assyria. The first half of the chapter takes that trust apart. Egypt's gods, river, economy and wisdom will all fail.

In the eighth century BC Egypt was divided. Several rival dynasties ruled different parts of the land, especially in the Nile delta, a period historians call the Third Intermediate Period. City against city and kingdom against kingdom fits that well. The Kushite king Piye marched north and subdued the rival rulers around 728 BC. The harsh masters of verse 4 have been identified with the Kushite conquerors, with the Assyrian kings who invaded Egypt in the 670s and 660s BC and sacked Thebes around 663 BC, or with later conquerors such as the Persians. The text names no one.

Egypt lived by the Nile. Its fishing, its flax and its famous fine linen all depended on the river's yearly flood. A dry Nile meant a ruined Egypt. The first hearers, who had been told by their leaders to lean on Egypt, were shown how little it could bear.
passages.later: God had said at the first exodus, ‘I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt’ (Exodus 12:12). And Isaiah warns those who ‘set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice’ (Isaiah 30:2).
passages.asks: Egypt's strength depended on a river that could fail. Ask what your security depends on, and what would happen if it dried up. And ask why the people of God kept leaning on Egypt anyway.

passages.happening:
‘The princes of Zoan are mere fools; Pharaoh’s wise counselors give senseless advice’ (verse 11). ‘Where are your wise men now?’ (verse 12). Let them tell what the LORD of Hosts has planned against Egypt.

The princes of Zoan and Memphis are deceived and have led Egypt astray (verse 13). The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion, so that Egypt staggers like a drunk (verse 14). There is nothing Egypt can do, head or tail, palm or reed (verse 15).

In that day the Egyptians will tremble with fear under the uplifted hand of the LORD of Hosts (verse 16). Judah will bring terror to Egypt, and Egypt will tremble whenever Judah is mentioned, because of what the LORD has planned (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Egypt was famous for its wisdom. Its court counselors and scribes were the envy of the ancient world, and Egypt's wisdom literature was old and admired. Isaiah says it has become foolishness. Zoan, or Tanis, was a royal city in the northeastern delta, and Memphis was the ancient capital near the apex of the delta.

The counselors claimed long lineages of wisdom. They cannot tell what God has planned. The first hearers were being warned against the wisdom of Judah's own counselors too, who kept urging an alliance with Egypt.

Verse 16 says the Egyptians will be like women, trembling with fear. In the speech of ancient war, this was a common picture of panic in soldiers. It describes fear in battle. It is not a statement about women.
passages.later: Jeremiah later says the same of Egypt and its gods: ‘I am about to punish Amon god of Thebes, along with Pharaoh, Egypt with her gods and kings, and those who trust in Pharaoh’ (Jeremiah 46:25).
passages.asks: Egypt's famous wisdom could not see what God planned. Ask whose wisdom you trust most, and whether it knows God. And ask where you have been confidently wrong.

passages.t: Egypt, Assyria and Israel worshiping together
passages.happening:
‘In that day five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts. One of them will be called the City of the Sun’ (verse 18).

There will be an altar to the LORD in the middle of Egypt and a pillar at its border (verse 19), a sign and a witness. ‘When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them’ (verse 20). The LORD will make himself known to Egypt, and Egypt will know the LORD and worship him (verse 21). He will strike Egypt, ‘but heal them’ (verse 22).

‘In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria’ (verse 23), and Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together. Israel will join them as the third, ‘a blessing upon the earth’ (verse 24). The LORD will speak over all three: “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This is among the most astonishing passages in the Old Testament. Egypt, the house of slavery from which God rescued Israel, has its own exodus story here. It cries out under oppressors, as Israel once cried out in Egypt, and God sends it a savior. And Assyria, the empire threatening Judah at that very moment, is named beside it as God's own.

The language of Canaan is Hebrew. The City of the Sun is probably Heliopolis near Memphis; most Hebrew manuscripts read City of Destruction, while the Dead Sea Isaiah Scroll and other witnesses read City of the Sun, which the BSB follows.

Jewish communities did settle in Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and a Jewish military colony at Elephantine on the southern border had its own temple in the fifth century BC. In the second century BC a Jewish priest named Onias built a temple at Leontopolis in the delta, and Josephus reports that he justified it from this chapter's altar in Egypt. Many scholars date some of verses 16 to 25 later than Isaiah for these reasons; others hold that the prophet saw the nations' conversion in a vision that no later event exhausts.

The titles God gives are the titles he gave Israel: his people, the work of his hands, his inheritance. The first hearers' greatest enemies are pictured as their fellow worshipers.
passages.later: The first exodus began when God said, ‘I have heard them crying out because of their oppressors’ (Exodus 3:7). A psalm sees the nations enrolled in Zion: ‘I will mention Rahab and Babylon among those who know Me’ (Psalm 87:4).
passages.hard:
Have verses 18 to 25 ever come true, or do they describe the future?

Readers give several answers. Some point to history in stages: Jewish communities in Egypt from the sixth century BC on, the Greek translation of the Scriptures made in Alexandria, and later the rise of Christianity in both Egypt and Mesopotamia, where churches flourished for centuries. Others read these verses as a vision of the final age, when the nations will worship God together, and hold that no period has fulfilled them fully. Some scholars read them as a later expansion reflecting the hopes of Jews in Egypt.

What is clear is the text's own horizon: in that day, a time of God's future action, the enemies of God's people become his people. These notes take no side on how it unfolds. They do not read these verses as a prediction about any nation or politics of the present day.
passages.asks: God calls Israel's oppressors his people and his handiwork. Ask who you would find it hardest to see worshiping beside you. And ask what it would mean for your enemies to become God's people, and so your family.
